title: 7 Steps to Responsive Tables
summary: This lesson demonstrates how to transform complex data tables for mobile devices by restructuring them into cards rather than simply shrinking them. It covers data prioritization, layout stacking, and using container queries for component-level responsiveness.

transcript.text: Your table on a phone. Don't shrink it, restructure it.
Six columns, three fit on one line. Which three? Not the leftmost. Rank by use: identity, value, state.
The ID leaves first. Nobody reads it on a phone.
Horizontal scroll hides half the row. Stack instead. Two lines per row. Name left, amount right. Status and due date underneath.
The row reads as one unit, thumb-sized.
Cards kill comparison. Amounts drift under names. Nothing lines up.
One slot for the amount. Top right every card, tabular figures. A list of cards is still a column of numbers.
No header row on a card. So label the ambiguous. March 4th alone means nothing. Due March 4th does.
A dollar amount needs no label. Sorting moves to a control.
Hidden isn't deleted. Tap the row. Invoice ID, notes, actions slide in.
Two fields, expand in place. A full record, bottom sheet. Never a new page for a glance.
The breakpoint belongs to the table, not the screen. Six columns need 700 pixels. Below that, cards.
One container query. Same table in a desktop side panel, cards too.
Six moves, done. Or type /restyle. UX Engine, the Claude code plugin that kills the AI look. Link in bio.

on_screen_text: Name left - Amount right - State below
Dates get a label. Dollars don't.
design_principles: Restructure rather than shrink for mobile
Rank data by Identity, Value, and State
Label ambiguous data (dates) but not obvious data (currency)
Use progressive disclosure for secondary details
Use container queries for component-level responsiveness
before_after: A 6-column desktop table shrunk to fit a mobile screen with tiny text and horizontal scrolling transformed into a restructured card-based layout with ranked data and progressive disclosure.
